title: Interval Between Injury and Surgery Influences Knee Biomechanics During Walking in Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstructed Patients: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) is commonly performed to restore anatomical and functional knee stability. Although altered walking biomechanics have been observed post-ACLR, previous studies have not consistently accounted for the interval between injury and surgery.
OBJECTIVE: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to determine whether walking-related knee biomechanical alterations following ACLR are transient or persist over time, and whether the timing of surgery influences these alterations.
METHODS: Five electronic databases (Scopus, PubMed, Web of Science, Physiotherapy Evidence Database [PEDro], and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials [CENTRAL]) were systematically searched from inception through August 2026. Studies comparing walking biomechanics between patients who underwent ACLR and healthy controls and reporting the interval between anterior cruciate ligament injury and reconstructive surgery were included. Biomechanical outcomes during the stance phase of walking were extracted and stratified according to the interval between injury and surgery: short term (0 to < 6 months), mid-term (6 to < 12 months), and long term (≥ 12 months). Standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals were calculated using a random-effects model. Study quality was assessed using a modified Downs and Black checklist.
RESULTS: Of the 3522 identified records, 16 studies involving male and female participants aged 18-55 years met the inclusion criteria. The mean methodological quality score was 65%, indicating an overall moderate level of methodological quality. Compared with healthy controls, ACLR participants demonstrated lower peak knee flexion angle (SMD = - 0.33, 95% confidence interval [CI] - 0.64 to - 0.02, p = 0.03, I2 = 57%), peak knee adduction angle (SMD = - 0.47, 95% CI - 0.92 to - 0.01, p = 0.04, I2 = 66%), and peak knee flexion moment (SMD = - 0.64, 95% CI - 1.05 to - 0.23, p = 0.002, I2 = 76%). In subgroup analyses, the long-term group (≥ 12 months between injury and surgery) demonstrated lower peak knee flexion angle (SMD = - 0.27, 95% CI - 0.54 to - 0.00, p = 0.05, I2 = 8%) and peak knee flexion moment (SMD = - 1.97, 95% CI - 3.77 to - 0.17, p = 0.03, I2 = 88%). The short-term group (0 to < 6 months) demonstrated lower peak knee adduction angle (SMD = - 0.79, 95% CI - 1.18 to - 0.40, p < 0.0001, I2 = 19%) and peak knee extension moment (SMD = - 0.55, 95% CI - 0.93 to - 0.18, p = 0.004, I2 = 50%).
CONCLUSIONS: The interval between anterior cruciate ligament injury and ACLR was associated with differences in postoperative walking biomechanics. Delayed reconstruction (≥ 12 months) is associated with persistent sagittal plane deficits, which may reflect chronic neuromuscular adaptations or preoperative joint degeneration. In contrast, early surgery (within 6 months after anterior cruciate ligament injury) was associated with fewer long-term sagittal-plane deficits, although temporary frontal-plane asymmetries and extension deficits may persist during the early postoperative period and may improve with rehabilitation. These findings underscore the importance of considering the timing of ACLR when planning surgery and postoperative rehabilitation to support walking recovery.

title: No Differences in Patient-reported Outcomes Between the Direct Anterior and Posterolateral Approach for THA: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The direct anterior approach (DAA) for THA is seeing wider use because it is purported to deliver a faster postoperative recovery. However, most previous studies comparing the DAA with the posterolateral approach (PLA) were limited by small sample sizes, heterogeneous patient populations, and the use of outcome measures with ceiling effects.
QUESTIONS/PURPOSES: (1) Does the DAA result in a higher proportion of patients achieving the patient acceptable symptom state (PASS) on the Hip Disability and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (HOOS) after THA compared with the PLA? (2) Are there differences in symptoms, physical function, life activities and participation, health-related quality of life (QoL), or complications between the DAA and PLA in the first postoperative year?
METHODS: A prospective, parallel-group, nonblinded, randomized controlled trial comparing the DAA and PLA for THA was conducted. Patients with primary or secondary osteoarthritis with an indication for THA with an uncemented femoral stem and cemented acetabular component were eligible. Of the 241 patients assessed for eligibility, 53% (128) were included in the study. Fifty-one percent (65 of 128) were randomized to the DAA group, and 49% (63 of 128) were randomized to the PLA group. One patient in each group was lost to follow-up, leaving 98% (64 of 65) and 98% (62 of 63) of patients available for analysis, respectively. There were no between-group differences in baseline or perioperative measurements. The primary outcome was achievement of the PASS on the HOOS at 3 months postoperatively. An a priori sample-size calculation indicated that 60 patients per group were required to detect a 20% difference in PASS achievement between groups (80% power; α = 0.05). With an expected loss to follow-up of 10%, the sample size was set to 65 patients per group. Secondary outcomes included symptoms, physical functioning, participation, and health-related QoL, assessed using patient-reported outcome measures and physical performance tests. Complications were assessed using the Clavien-Dindo classification. Outcomes were assessed preoperatively as well as at 2 weeks, 6 weeks, 3 months, and 1 year postoperatively.
RESULTS: At 3 months, the proportion of patients achieving the PASS did not differ between the DAA and PLA for any HOOS subscales, including symptoms (65% [41 of 63] versus 63% [39 of 62], OR 1.03 [95% confidence interval (CI) 0.80 to 1.35]; p = 0.80), pain (48% [30 of 63] versus 53% [33 of 62], OR 0.90 [95% CI 0.63 to 1.27]; p = 0.53), activities of daily living (68% [43 of 63] versus 65% [40 of 62], OR 1.06 [95% CI 0.82 to 1.36]; p = 0.66), sports and recreation (55% [34 of 62] versus 58% [36 of 62], OR 0.94 [95% CI 0.69 to 1.29]; p = 0.72), and QoL (73% [46 of 63] versus 71% [44 of 62], OR 1.03 [95% CI 0.83 to 1.28]; p = 0.80). There were no between-group differences in symptoms, physical function, life activities and participation, and health-related QoL at any time point. Complications occurred in 8% (5 of 65) of patients in the DAA group and 2% (1 of 63) of patients in the PLA group (OR 3.05 [95% CI 0.51 to 18.40]; p = 0.21).
CONCLUSION: In this randomized controlled trial, the DAA did not improve patient-reported or functional outcomes compared with the PLA during the first postoperative year. In the absence of demonstrated patient-reported or functional benefits of the DAA, surgeons should not represent to patients that the DAA provides advantages in terms of the pace or magnitude of recovery. Future studies powered to detect differences in the risk of complications should be performed to see whether harms are more likely with the DAA than with other surgical approaches.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I, therapeutic study.

title: Is the number of strength and hop tests passed at the time of return to pre-injury sport level associated with second ACL injury? A registry study of 458 patients.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To analyze whether the number of strength and hop tests passed in a 5-test battery was associated with the hazard of second ACL injury after returning to pre-injury level of sports (RTS).
DESIGN: Registry-based cohort study.
SETTING: Data extracted in February 2026 from a rehabilitation registry.
PARTICIPANTS: Patients aged 15-35 years at the time of primary ACL reconstruction with ipsilateral hamstring or patellar tendon autograft and pre-injury Tegner activity level ≥ 6.
MAIN OUTCOME MEASURE: Second ACL injury after RTS, assessed during available follow-up and within one year of RTS using a Cox proportional hazard regression model. Hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals were calculated and p-value was set to < 0.05.
RESULTS: 458 patients were included. 60 (13%) second ACL injuries occurred within all available follow-up time, where 32 (7.0%) occurred within 1 year after RTS. No significant association was observed between number of tests passed and second ACL injury during available follow-up (p = 0.41), or within one year of RTS (p = 0.87), after adjustment for autograft type, time to RTS, and BMI.
CONCLUSION: The number of tests passed in a 5-test muscle function battery was not associated with the hazard of second ACL injury after RTS.

title: Minimally Invasive Zadek Osteotomy vs Open Achilles Debridement for Insertional Achilles Tendinopathy in Athletes: A Retrospective Comparative Cohort Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Insertional Achilles tendinopathy (IAT) is a common cause of posterior heel pain in athletic populations and may require surgical intervention following failed conservative management. Minimally invasive Zadek osteotomy (MIS Zadek) has emerged as an alternative to traditional open Achilles tendon debridement with Haglund resection, with potential advantages in recovery and complication profile.
METHODS: A retrospective comparative cohort study was performed including 50 athletic patients with IAT (25 MIS Zadek, 25 open surgery) treated between 2022 and 2024 at a single high-volume centre. All patients participated in regular sports activity and failed at least 6 months of nonoperative treatment. The primary outcome was time to return to sport. Secondary outcomes included return-to-sport rate, Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) physical function (PF), PROMIS pain interference (PI), and postoperative complications. Multivariable regression analysis was performed to adjust for potential confounders.
RESULTS: Return to sport was achieved in 100% of MIS patients (25/25) and 92% of open patients (23/25; P = .49). Time to return to sport was shorter following MIS Zadek (4.3 ± 1.2 vs 6.1 ± 1.5 months; mean difference -1.8 months, 95% CI -2.6 to -1.0; P < .001). MIS remained independently associated with faster return to sport (adjusted β = -1.6 months, 95% CI -2.4 to -0.8; P < .001). Both groups showed substantial and clinically meaningful improvements in PROMIS outcomes. At 6 months, PROMIS PF was higher in the MIS group (56.5 ± 5.8 vs 52.3 ± 6.4; mean difference +4.2, 95% CI 0.6-7.8; P = .02; Cohen d = 0.69), with a similar pattern for PROMIS PI (47.2 ± 5.5 vs 51.1 ± 6.0; mean difference -3.9, 95% CI -7.1 to -0.7; P = .02; Cohen d = 0.67). By 18 months, PROMIS PF improved further in both groups with comparable outcomes (59.4 ± 4.9 vs 57.8 ± 5.2; mean difference +1.6, 95% CI -1.4 to 4.6; P = .29), and PROMIS PI similarly converged (44.8 ± 4.9 vs 46.3 ± 5.1; mean difference -1.5, 95% CI -4.4 to 1.4; P = .30). Complication rates were lower in the MIS group (2/25, 8%) compared with the open group (6/25, 24%; P = .25), although this difference did not reach statistical significance.
CONCLUSION: MIS Zadek osteotomy was associated with faster return to sport and improved early recovery compared with open surgery; with the numbers available, no significant difference in long-term functional outcomes could be detected. Complications were numerically less frequent following MIS Zadek osteotomy, although this difference did not reach statistical significanceLevel of Evidence:Level III, retrospective comparative cohort study.

title: Efficacy and safety study of diclofenac epolamine topical patch in accelerating rehabilitation of moderate hamstring strain: A randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Moderate hamstring strain is a common sports injury impairing daily and athletic function. While topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) offer localized pain relief with reduced systemic effects, high-quality evidence specific to hamstring injury is limited.
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the effect of a short-course topical diclofenac epolamine patch combined with rehabilitation on pain and functional recovery in moderate hamstring strain.
METHODS: In this single-center, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 120 patients were randomized to an experimental group (diclofenac patch twice daily for 14 days plus rehabilitation) or a control group (placebo patch plus identical rehabilitation). Outcomes assessed included pain measured by the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), as the primary endpoint, muscle strength, knee range of motion (ROM), functional back-kick test, time to rehabilitation criteria and safety (adverse events, liver/renal function).
RESULTS: The diclofenac group demonstrated significantly greater pain reduction at days 14, 21 and 28 post-intervention (all p < 0.01). Muscle strength recovery was superior at days 21 and 28, knee ROM improved more at day 28 and functional back-kick performance was better at day 28 (all p < 0.05). Time to meet rehabilitation criteria was significantly shorter in the experimental group (p = 0.002). Adverse event incidence and changes in liver/renal function were similar between groups (all p > 0.05).
CONCLUSION: A short-course topical diclofenac epolamine patch, combined with rehabilitation training, effectively alleviates pain, accelerates functional recovery, and is safe for treating moderate hamstring strain, supporting its use in clinical and sports rehabilitation.

title: Effects of caffeine supplementation on exercise-induced muscle damage: A systematic review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) commonly occurs following unaccustomed or high-intensity exercise and is characterized by delayed-onset muscle soreness, elevated muscle damage biomarkers, and transient declines in muscle function. Caffeine, a widely consumed ergogenic aid, has been proposed to mitigate these adverse effects; however, the evidence across studies remains equivocal. This systematic review aimed to synthesize findings from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that investigated the effects of caffeine supplementation on markers of EIMD.
METHODS: Following preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses guidelines, a comprehensive search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar databases, supplemented by citation tracking. RCTs published between 2005 and 2025 that included human participants and reported direct or indirect indicators of EIMD were eligible. Fifteen RCTs (n = 222) were included and assessed for methodological quality using the PEDro scale.
RESULTS: Caffeine doses ranged from 3 to 6 mg/kg. Among the 6 studies assessing delayed-onset muscle soreness, 4 reported significant reductions in perceived soreness within 24 to 48 hours post-exercise, whereas 2 found no effect or adverse responses. Eleven studies examined biochemical markers; most detected no significant differences between caffeine and placebo, while 2 observed higher creatine kinase levels in the caffeine group. Five studies evaluated functional performance; some indicated attenuation of decrements in maximal voluntary isometric contraction or isokinetic torque, although results were inconsistent.
CONCLUSION: Caffeine supplementation may transiently reduce subjective muscle soreness and, under certain conditions, help preserve muscle function following EIMD, but its effects on biochemical markers are inconsistent. The overall efficacy appears to depend on factors such as exercise modality, dosage, timing, and inter-individual variability. Larger, well-controlled RCTs with standardized protocols are needed to clarify caffeine's role in muscle damage and recovery.

title: Gracilis tendon harvest for ACL reconstruction impairs gracilis muscle volume recovery and may adversely affect adjacent thigh musculature. MRI-based outcomes from a subgroup of patients enroled in the DOSTAR randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Segmentation of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) allows accurate calculation of muscle volumes. The Dual Or Single Tendon Anterior cruciate ligament Reconstruction (DOSTAR) study is a prospective randomized controlled trial investigating a semitendinosus (ST) graft with adjustable button tibial fixation versus a dual tendon semitendinosus and gracilis (STG) graft with screw tibial fixation in anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR). The purpose of the present study is to investigate differences in thigh muscle volume at 6 and 12 months between these treatment groups.
METHODS: Patients were randomized and underwent ACLR using either a ST or STG graft construct. MRI of bilateral thighs was completed at 6 and 12 months post-operatively. Muscle volumes were measured in both thighs at both time points in both groups.
RESULTS: A total of 38 patients underwent MRI scanning at 6 and 12 months. There was a significant difference in the interval volume change of gracilis in the STG group compared to the ST group (-1.6 cm3 ± 4.6 vs. +2.8 cm3 ± 6.8, p = 0.026). Interval gracilis hypertrophy occurred in 35% (7/20) of cases in the STG group and 67% of cases (12/18) in the ST group (p = 0.103). Adductor longus (AddL) also demonstrated a significant difference in interval volume change between the STG and ST group (-2.4 cm3 ± 12.0 vs. +11.1 cm3 ± 21.2, p = 0.020). AddL hypertrophy occurred in 30% of cases (6/20) in the STG group and 72% (13/18) in the ST group (p = 0.022). All other muscles had no significant differences noted in muscle recovery between groups. Linear regression analysis demonstrated a significant positive relationship between interval changes in gracilis and AddL volumes (p < 0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: The present study provides MRI evidence that gracilis tendon harvest was associated with persistent impairment of gracilis muscle recovery and may also adversely affect AddL. This adds to the growing body of evidence supporting the use of ST with adjustable button graft constructs for hamstring ACLR.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level II, subgroup analysis of prospective, double-blinded, randomized controlled trial.

title: Prospective Polynomial Characterization of Tibial Plateau Geometry Shows No Association With Contralateral ACL Injury in Female Athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries are common in athletic people, with young female athletes at particularly high risk. After ACL injury, reconstruction, and return to sport, many sustain contralateral ACL (CACL) injuries. While tibial plateau cartilage surface geometry has been associated with first-time ACL injury risk, its role in subsequent CACL injury remains unclear.
HYPOTHESIS: The normal knee of female athletes who suffered a first-time ACL injury, underwent reconstruction, returned to preinjury activities and subsequently suffered a CACL injury will have tibial plateau cartilage surface geometry that is different compared with an equivalent population who did not sustain a subsequent CACL injury.
STUDY DESIGN: Prospective cohort study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 2.
METHODS: A total of 199 subjects who suffered a first-time ACL injury, had reconstruction, returned to preinjury activities and had a contralateral knee that was normal underwent bilateral magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan acquisitions. Tibial plateau cartilage geometry was assessed on the uninjured, normal knees using T1-weighted Fast Field Echo MRI. Parasagittal slices at maximum cartilage concavity in medial and lateral compartments of the tibia were characterized by fitting fifth-order polynomials. Female athletes who sustained a CACL injury within 4 years of reconstruction and return to sport (n = 12) were matched and compared with a group of female athletes who did not sustain CACL injury (n = 24). Random coefficient mixed-effects regression was used to assess group differences in polynomial functions.
RESULTS: No significant differences in tibial cartilage surface geometry were found between the first-time ACL and first-time ACL + CACL injury groups in the medial (P = 0.23) and lateral (P = 0.18) compartments.
CONCLUSION: These findings suggest that characterization of tibial plateau cartilage geometry in the normal knee of subjects who underwent reconstruction after a first-time ACL injury is insufficient to predict who will on go on to suffer a subsequent CACL injury.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: More comprehensive predictive models incorporating anatomic, biomechanical, and psychological factors are likely needed to identify those at increased risk for CACL injury after a first-time ACL injury and reconstruction.
topics: Return to sport and injury prevention

title: Effectiveness of a Structured Post-Platelet Rich Plasma Rehabilitation Approach on Pain and Function in Subacromial Pain Syndrome: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Subacromial pain syndrome (SAPS) causes pain and functional limitation. Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) is increasingly used as a supportive treatment. Optimal rehabilitation after PRP is unclear. This study investigated the effectiveness of a structured post-PRP rehabilitation approach on pain and function.
METHODS: Sixty participants with SAPS were randomized to two groups; 54 completed the study and were included in the final per-protocol analysis (27 per group). During a 21-day period, the study group received a structured post-PRP rehabilitation approach in addition to standard conventional physiotherapy, while the control group received standard conventional physiotherapy alone. Range of motion, muscle strength, and posture were evaluated. In addition, outcome measures included the Short-Form McGill Pain Questionnaire (SF-MPQ), Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand Questionnaire (DASH), Functional Impairment Test-Hand and Neck/Shoulder/Arm (FIT-HaNSA) and Constant-Murley Shoulder Score, which were administered for assessment purposes.
RESULTS: Corbin Posture Scale scores decreased in both groups (p < 0.05). Pain reduction was greater in the study group (VAS: from 9.00 ± 0.67 to 2.92 ± 1.14 versus from 9.11 ± 0.64 to 7.96 ± 0.75; SF-MPQ: from 27.07 ± 4.41 to 10.07 ± 3.33 versus from 21.33 ± 2.46 to 19.37 ± 2.35; p < 0.001). Improvements in Constant-Murley, DASH, and FIT-HaNSA scores, shoulder muscle strength, and active and passive range of motion were significantly greater in the study group (p < 0.001).
DISCUSSION: Adding a structured post-PRP rehabilitation approach to standard conventional physiotherapy may provide additional short-term improvements in pain, muscle strength, range of motion, and shoulder function compared with standard conventional physiotherapy alone in individuals with SAPS. However, long-term follow-up was not conducted. Therefore, the sustainability of the observed improvements remains unclear. Future studies should investigate the long-term effects of structured post-PRP rehabilitation approaches.

title: Return-to-Play Outcomes After Primary Ulnar Collateral Ligament Reconstruction Vary Substantially Depending on Return Criteria: A Systematic Review Stratified by Competition Level.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To determine how return definitions influence return to play (RTP), return to the same level of play (RTSP), advancement rates, and return timelines after primary ulnar collateral ligament reconstruction (UCLR) in baseball pitchers across levels of competition.
METHODS: Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, PubMed and Embase were searched from January 2000 to January 2025. Studies evaluating baseball pitchers undergoing primary UCLR and reporting RTP, RTSP, advancement, or return timing outcomes with participation-based (RTP based on a single event) or durability-based (RTP after sustained participation over a predefined threshold) criteria were included. Primary outcomes were RTP, RTSP, and advancement rate (progression to a higher level after UCLR); secondary outcome was return time stratified by return criteria. Risk of bias was assessed with the Methodological Index for Non-randomized Studies and Risk Of Bias in Non-randomized Studies of Interventions tools.
RESULTS: Twenty-four studies met inclusion. Across these studies, 19 included Major League Baseball players (2194 players), 5 included Minor League Baseball (MiLB) players (2318 players), 4 included collegiate athletes (553 athletes), and 6 included high school athletes (258 athletes). RTP/RTSP rates were 86% to 92%/70% to 87% in high school, 84%/67% to 92% in college, 76.3% to 79%/69.1% to 100% in MiLB, and 80% to 97.2%/28.1% to 87% in Major League Baseball. Advancement was 55.7% to 63.2% in high school, 4.1% to 44.4% in college, and 22.3% to 45% in MiLB. Surgery-to-return time using the common RTSP definition ranged from 13.7 to 20.5 months (Major League Baseball), 14.6 to 16.4 (MiLB), and 11 to 17 (college and high school). Durability-based definitions were not consistently associated with longer return intervals.
CONCLUSIONS: Without standardized return criteria, reported RTP, RTSP, advancement rates, and return timelines after primary UCLR in baseball pitchers varied substantially across studies and competition levels. Durability-based criteria were not consistently associated with longer return timelines, indicating that return outcomes should be interpreted according to the competition level and return definition used. Standardized, tier-specific return criteria may improve clinical interpretation after primary UCLR.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, systematic review of Level II to IV studies.

title: A Study of Functional Outcome of Arthroscopic Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Using Hamstring Graft.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury is a common cause of knee instability and functional limitation. Arthroscopic reconstruction using hamstring tendon autografts is widely used because of favorable functional outcomes and lower donor-site morbidity.
AIM: This study aims to evaluate the clinical and functional outcomes of patients undergoing arthroscopic ACL reconstruction using a hamstring tendon autograft.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: A prospective observational study was conducted over 18 months in the Department of Orthopaedics, M.G.M. Medical College and L.S.K. Hospital, Kishanganj, Bihar. Fifty patients aged 18-50 years with clinically and radiologically confirmed ACL tears underwent primary arthroscopic ACL reconstruction using a quadrupled hamstring tendon autograft. Femoral fixation was performed using a cortical button and tibial fixation using an interference screw. Patients were followed at 1, 2, 3, 6, and 12 months. Functional outcome was assessed using the Lysholm Knee Scoring Scale, while clinical stability and post-operative complications were documented. No comparator group was included. The study was confined to one institution, and no instrumented laxity measurements or formal return-to-sport outcomes were reported.
RESULTS: The mean age of participants was 31.72 ± 8.88 years, and 72% were male. Road traffic accidents were the commonest mechanism of injury (44%), followed by sports-related injuries (36%). Medial meniscal tear was the most common associated injury (40%). Fifteen of 50 patients (30%) experienced a recorded post-operative complication. In the total cohort, anterior knee pain occurred in 5/50 (10%), tunnel widening in 4/50 (8%), infection in 3/50 (6%), and tibial screw dislodgement, graft failure, and knee stiffness in 1/50 (2%) each. The mean Lysholm score improved from 50.74 ± 6.342 preoperatively to 86.00 ± 10.067 postoperatively (P < 0.05); 52% had good, and 32% had excellent Lysholm outcomes at final follow-up.
CONCLUSION: In this single-center prospective observational cohort of 50 patients, Lysholm scores improved over 12 months after hamstring autograft ACL reconstruction, with 84% classified as having good-to-excellent outcomes. These findings describe short-term recovery within the treated cohort. The absence of a comparator and adjusted analyses precludes causal attribution or conclusions about superiority over alternative reconstruction strategies or non-operative management; long-term effectiveness and return to sport were not established.

title: Selective recovery effects of short-term beetroot juice supplementation after exercise-induced muscle damage in trained female volleyball players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Beetroot juice (BRJ) has been proposed as a nutritional aid for recovery from exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD), but evidence in female team-sport athletes is limited. It also remains unclear whether any benefit extends across functional, pain-related, swelling, and strength outcomes.
METHODS: Seventeen female university volleyball players entered a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial. Four did not complete the second period, so outcomes were analyzed with linear mixed models. After baseline testing, participants performed 200 loaded vertical jumps and consumed BRJ or placebo at 24, 48, and 72 h post-EIMD. Recovery outcomes were countermovement jump (CMJ) height, volleyball-specific agility time, pressure pain threshold, thigh circumference, visual analog scale soreness, and knee isokinetic measures. Holm-adjusted planned contrasts were used.
RESULTS: CMJ height was the clearest BRJ-related functional finding. The treatment × time interaction showed a trend toward statistical significance (P = 0.062), and CMJ height was higher under BRJ than PLA at 72 h post-EIMD (P = 0.033, d = 1.01). Calf pressure pain threshold also favored BRJ at 72 h, accompanied by a significant treatment × time interaction (P < 0.001). In contrast, agility time and soreness changed over time without clear between-condition differences, while thigh pressure pain threshold, thigh circumference, and low-velocity knee isokinetic outcomes showed no consistent BRJ-related advantage.
CONCLUSIONS: Short-term BRJ supplementation was associated with selective rather than generalized recovery benefits after EIMD in trained female volleyball players. The clearest findings were higher CMJ height and calf PPT under BRJ than PLA at 72 h, whereas the remaining outcomes showed no consistent treatment-related differences.

title: Multi-planar patellar hypomobility as a potential contributor to VMO-VL dyssynergy and return to sport limitations following ACL reconstruction in soccer players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patellofemoral hypomobility (PFH) is a frequent yet underestimated complication following anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction. PFH induces biomechanical and neuromuscular alterations that impair return to sport (RTS) and accelerate early joint degeneration. However, current evidence describes PFH primarily as an associated factor rather than a direct causal determinant of RTS failure. Therefore, the primary objective of this review is to analyze the correlation between PFH and functional complications during RTS. The study also aims to summarize the available evidence on the relationship between PFH and medium- to long-term clinical outcomes, without implying causal predictions where not supported.
METHODS: A narrative review was conducted across PubMed, EMBASE, Scopus, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), and Web of Science using a Population, Intervention, Comparison, and Outcome (PICO)-structured search. No systematic review procedures or pooled quantitative analyses were performed; all numerical data derived from individual studies. Included studies involved athletes aged 18-35 undergoing primary ACL reconstruction with Bone-Patellar Tendon-Bone (BPTB) or Hamstring autografts.
RESULTS: The analysis reveals significant PFH (>25% compared to the contralateral side) in 15-22% of athletes at 6 months, with a peak of 28% in BPTB graft cases. Longitudinal hypomobility correlates with extension deficit, whereas transverse hypomobility is associated with increased anterior knee pain (AKP) in 34% of cases. Data indicate a 12-15% reduction in Countermovement Jump (CMJ) performance and a 3.4-fold higher risk of patellofemoral osteoarthritis (PFOA) within 5 years, although PFH was not directly measured as an independent variable in these studies. Additionally, 25% of athletes with PFH discontinue competitive activity within 36 months after RTS.
CONCLUSIONS: PFH emerges as an important factor associated with postoperative functional limitations. Restricted patellar glide disrupts the vastus medialis obliquus (VMO)/vastus lateralis (VL) synergy, reduces performance, and accelerates cartilage degeneration. Symmetry of patellar kinematics should be considered a relevant parameter for RTS decision-making, while acknowledging that RTS outcomes are multifactorial and not solely determined by PFH.

title: Greater eccentric hamstrings to concentric quadriceps strength ratio at 6 months after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction is associated with reduced odds of revision within 2 years.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To investigate the association between eccentric hamstrings-to-concentric quadriceps strength ratio (mixed hamstrings to quadriceps [HQ]-strength ratio) at 6 months postoperatively and revision anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACL-R) within 2 years of primary surgery. The secondary purpose was to investigate the association between the mixed HQ-strength ratio and single-leg hop for distance limb symmetry index (LSI).
METHODS: Data were collected from a local registry at Capio Artro Clinic, Stockholm, Sweden. Patients aged ≥15 years, without concomitant ligament injuries and meniscal resection or repair who underwent primary ACL-R with hamstring tendon autografts between 2005 and 2021 were included. Isokinetic eccentric hamstrings and concentric quadriceps strength were assessed using a Biodex dynamometer 6 months postoperatively. Associations between mixed HQ-strength ratio on the ACL-R leg and revision ACL-R were analysed using multivariable logistic regression analysis, presented with odds ratios (ORs), 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and area under the receiver operating characteristics curve (AUC). Associations between mixed HQ-strength ratio and single-leg hop for distance LSI were analysed with linear regression.
RESULTS: Of the 3458 patients included, 49.5% were female and the mean age was 28.8 ± 10.4 years. Patients who underwent revision ACL-R within 2 years had lower mixed HQ-strength ratio on the ACL-R leg 6 months postoperatively. After adjustment for age at primary ACL-R and preinjury Tegner level, each 10-unit increase in the mixed HQ-strength ratio on the ACL-R leg was associated with lower odds of revision ACL-R (OR = 0.81, 95% CI [0.71;0.93], p = 0.003). However, the discriminatory ability was poor (AUC = 0.64). A greater mixed HQ-strength ratio was associated with poorer single-leg hop for distance LSI, adjusted for age at primary ACL-R and preinjury Tegner level (β = -1.30, 95% CI [-1.51;-1.09], p < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: The mixed HQ-strength ratio may complement the evaluation of muscle strength recovery after ACL-R. However, its poor discriminatory ability limits its use to identify patients who will undergo revision ACL-R.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

title: Effects of vitamin D supplementation on vitamin D status and physical performance in football players: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Low vitamin D status is frequently reported among athletes, but whether vitamin D supplementation improves physical performance in football players remains uncertain. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the effects of vitamin D supplementation on serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] concentration, jump performance, sprint performance, aerobic capacity, and muscular performance in association football and futsal players.
METHODS: PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from database inception to 31 May 2026. Controlled intervention studies comparing vitamin D supplementation with control conditions were eligible. Standardized mean differences were calculated as Hedges' g and pooled using random-effects meta-analyses. Two reviewers independently extracted data and assessed risk of bias using RoB 2 or ROBINS-I. The certainty of evidence was assessed using GRADE. The protocol was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261430873).
RESULTS: Eleven reports representing nine independent studies and 312 players were included. In RCT-only primary analyses, vitamin D supplementation was associated with higher circulating 25(OH)D concentrations (g = 1.41, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.92; I² = 58.0%). Pooled effects were not statistically significant for jump performance (g = 0.21, 95% CI -0.10 to 0.53), sprint performance (g = -0.03, 95% CI -0.40 to 0.34), aerobic capacity (g = 0.00, 95% CI -0.45 to 0.45), or muscular performance (g = 0.19, 95% CI -0.14 to 0.51). The certainty of evidence was low for circulating 25(OH)D, jump performance, and muscular performance, and very low for sprint performance and aerobic capacity.
CONCLUSIONS: Vitamin D supplementation was associated with increased circulating 25(OH)D concentrations, whereas current evidence is insufficient to support a consistent improvement in physical performance. Given the low to very low certainty of evidence, these findings should be interpreted cautiously. Larger, well-designed randomized controlled trials using standardized, football-relevant performance tests are warranted.

title: Efficacy of combined therapies on degenerative joint disease of the temporomandibular joint: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the efficacy of intra-articular orthobiologics versus standard active control (arthrocentesis or hyaluronic acid) on pain, mouth opening and structural bone gain in advanced degenerative temporomandibular joint (TMJ) disease, stratified by orthobiologic class and joint compartment.
DESIGN: Systematic review with exploratory meta-analysis, following PRISMA and prospectively registered on PROSPERO (CRD420261425634), of RCTs published January 2020-June 2026. Outcomes were pooled as mean difference (MD) by orthobiologic class, with joint compartment as a three-level moderator. Clinical relevance was assessed against minimal important difference (MCID) thresholds; non-randomised studies were synthesised narratively.
RESULTS: Twenty-eight studies were included: 18 RCTs (≈862 patients; 12 pooled) and 10 narrative studies. Versus hyaluronic acid, orthobiologics reduced pain (MD -0.71) and improved mouth opening (MD 3.04 mm), both below the MCID. Versus arthrocentesis alone, effects were larger: pain (MD -1.57, exceeding the MCID) and mouth opening (MD 3.46 mm, below the MCID), with high heterogeneity unexplained by orthobiologic class. No RCT tested the dual joint space approach, represented only by one narrative study. A subset of studies had incomplete degenerative anchoring or unreported compartment. Certainty of evidence was low to very low.
CONCLUSIONS: Current evidence does not support a firm recommendation for any single orthobiologic in advanced degenerative TMJ disease, reinforcing a conservative, stepwise approach. Dual joint space therapy - a plausible but untested hypothesis - remains unstudied and is a priority for future research.

title: Association between sleep difficulty and baseline concussion-like symptom burden in NCAA Division I athletes.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To examine the association between sleep difficulty and baseline concussion-like symptom burden among NCAA Division I athletes and whether sleep difficulty is associated with neurocognitive performance.
METHODS: This cross-sectional analysis included 584 NCAA Division I student-athletes. Sleep difficulty was assessed using the Athlete Sleep Screening Questionnaire Sleep Difficulty Score (SDS), and symptom burden using the 24-item SCOAT6 Symptom Evaluation. Symptom number was analyzed with multivariable negative binomial regression and symptom severity with multivariable linear regression using HC3 robust standard errors. Models adjusted for age, sex, sport type, and head-injury history. Sensitivity analyses excluded overlapping sleep-related symptoms and examined individual symptoms, symptom domains, head-injury strata, and neurocognitive outcomes.
RESULTS: Each 1-point increase in SDS was associated with greater symptom number (n = 583; IRR = 1.127, 95% CI 1.086-1.169, P < .001) and severity (n = 584; B = 1.054, 95% CI 0.688-1.419, P < .001). Associations persisted after excluding sleep disturbance and after additionally excluding fatigue/low energy and drowsiness. Twenty-one of 24 symptoms remained associated with SDS after false-discovery-rate correction. Head-injury history did not modify associations with symptom number (P = .971) or severity (P = .846). SDS was not associated with memory (B = -0.012, P = .269), executive function (B = -0.017, P = .247), or psychomotor speed (B = 0.001, P = .939).
CONCLUSIONS: Greater self-reported sleep difficulty was associated with greater baseline concussion-like symptom burden but not with assessed neurocognitive outcomes. Sleep difficulty should be considered a contextual factor when interpreting baseline concussion symptom reports.

title: Outcomes of open and endoscopic excision of a symptomatic os trigonum in athletes: a systematic review with exploratory analysis of prognostic factors.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: A symptomatic os trigonum causes posterior ankle impingement in athletes and is excised when conservative treatment fails. Previous syntheses have pooled mean outcomes across mixed populations, and poor outcomes have not been defined consistently.
METHODS: Six databases were searched for open or endoscopic os trigonum excision in athletes, following PRISMA 2020 and SWiM. Techniques were compared within comparative studies, with supplementary pooling. A composite poor-outcome profile and eight candidate factors were examined at study-arm level.
RESULTS: Thirteen studies (17 arms, 440 participants) were included. Failure to return to prior level was uncommon (9 of 438; 0-6.2% by arm). In the randomised trial, return to prior sport level was 4.4 weeks faster after endoscopic excision (95% confidence interval [CI] 2.7-6.1); pooling two further non-randomised studies with imputed SDs gave 4.9 weeks (95% CI 3.3-6.6). Trial complications occurred in 1 of 26 endoscopic and 6 of 26 open patients (odds ratio 7.50, 95% CI 0.83-67.49); the two-study pooled odds ratio was 5.59 (95% CI 1.10-28.35) from 10 events. Both nerve injuries described as permanent followed open surgery. The composite depended on arm size and threshold choice, and five of eight candidate factors could not be tested.
CONCLUSION: Poor outcomes are uncommon after either approach. Low-certainty evidence suggests faster return to sport after endoscopic excision; complication evidence is of very low certainty, though no nerve injury described as permanent followed endoscopic excision. A consensus definition of return to sport is needed.

title: Risk, Knowledge, and Awareness of Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S) in Elite Female Volleyball Players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S) is a condition caused by low energy availability (LEA) and is associated with adverse health and performance outcomes in athletes. Although volleyball involves considerable physical stress and repetitive jumping, little is known about RED-S knowledge and risk of LEA in elite female volleyball players.
HYPOTHESIS: Elite female volleyball athletes have limited awareness of RED-S, and athletes at risk for LEA according to the LEAF-Q are more likely to be injured.
STUDY DESIGN: Cross-sectional study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.
METHODS: Elite female volleyball athletes competing in the Turkish Women's Elite Volleyball League during the 2024-2025 season were recruited. Participants completed an online survey including demographic information, the Low Energy Availability in Females Questionnaire (LEAF-Q), and items assessing knowledge, awareness, and support-seeking behaviors related to RED-S. Athletes were classified as "at risk" for LEA using a LEAF-Q cutoff score of ≥8. Associations between LEAF-Q risk status and injury history during the previous year were analyzed.
RESULTS: A total of 148 athletes participated. The mean LEAF-Q score was 5.50 ± 3.48, and 25% of athletes were classified as at risk for LEA according to the LEAF-Q. Most athletes (92.6%) reported never having heard of RED-S or the Female Athlete Triad. Athletes identified as at risk by the LEAF-Q were significantly more likely to have sustained an injury in the previous year than athletes not at risk (odds ratio, 7.86; 95% CI, 3.03-20.41).
CONCLUSION: Elite female volleyball athletes demonstrated low knowledge of RED-S, while a substantial proportion were identified as at risk for LEA. LEA risk was associated strongly with injury history, supporting the clinical relevance of LEAF-Q screening in this population.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Routine LEAF-Q screening combined with sport-specific education may facilitate early identification of athletes who may require further clinical evaluation for LEA-related problems and may inform prevention-oriented support strategies in elite female volleyball players.

title: Male-female differences in unilateral jump-landing energetics are concentrated in propulsion-phase work generation across self-paced and ball-interception tasks in competitive soccer players.
abstract:
PURPOSE: This cross-sectional observational study compared jump performance and braking-, propulsion- and landing-phase energetics during self-paced hands-on-hips single-leg countermovement jump (SL-CMJ) and soccer-relevant jump-heading-landing (SR-JHL) between sampled male and female competitive soccer players. A secondary aim examined associations between propulsion-phase knee positive work (generation) and jump height.
METHODS: Forty-five players (22 males, 18.4 ± 2.1 years; 23 females, 20.1 ± 3.5 years) performed SL-CMJ and SR-JHL bilaterally using force plates and three-dimensional motion capture. SR-JHL incorporated a large-screen interactive soccer scene, real-time marker-driven avatar, unrestricted arms, height-scaled virtual-ball heading and tested-limb landing. Limb-averaged outcomes included jump performance, modified reactive strength index (RSI-mod), phase-specific center-of-mass and hip-knee-ankle work and relative joint contribution. Welch tests, Hedges' g and false discovery rate (FDR) correction compared sexes within tasks; mixed-effects models examined knee energetics-jump height associations.
RESULTS: Males had greater jump height and RSI-mod in both tasks (g = 1.34-2.85; q < 0.001), greater propulsion-phase center-of-mass generation and jump center-of-mass net work (g = 0.68-1.35; q ≤ 0.033); however, braking or landing center-of-mass absorption did not differ significantly between groups after FDR correction. Males also showed greater propulsion-phase knee generation, lower ankle generation share, higher knee generation share and greater landing knee absorption. Absolute propulsion-phase knee generation was associated with jump height after accounting for sex and task (β = 0.0147 m per standard deviation; p = 0.042), with a stronger association in SR-JHL (p = 0.006).
CONCLUSION: Differences between the sampled male and female cohorts were concentrated in propulsion-phase work generation, with greater hip and knee work in the male cohort and greater ankle contribution in the female cohort. Propulsion-phase knee positive work was associated with jump height, particularly in SR-JHL. Because sex was inseparable from cohort context, these findings describe between-group differences-not independent sex effects-and provide task-specific comparison context for future anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction and return-to-sport research.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

title: Severe injuries in competitive cycling during an olympic cycle: injury patterns, time loss, and return-to-performance outcomes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cycling is an established Olympic sport associated with a distinct injury profile that has not yet been comprehensively investigated. This study aimed to retrospectively assess and analyze severe cycling-related injuries resulting in ≥ 3 weeks of time loss over a complete Olympic cycle.
METHODS: A total of 192 cyclists were included, based on a retrospective online questionnaire assessing injury location, type, context, time loss, and return-to-sport outcomes. Comparisons by sex, discipline, and competitive level were performed at the athlete level using exact tests with 95% confidence intervals and were considered exploratory.
RESULTS: Seventy-two of 192 athletes sustained at least one severe injury over the five-year period, corresponding to a proportion of 37.5% (95% CI 31.0-44.5). A total of 237 injuries were recorded, with the upper extremity (33.8%) and lower extremity (27.8%) being the most frequently affected regions. The most common diagnoses were hand fractures (n = 14), clavicle fractures (n = 13), and non-specific knee injuries (n = 9). Hand fractures (33.3%; p = 0.002) and shoulder dislocations (20.0%; p = 0.002) were most frequent among BMX athletes, while hand fractures also occurred more frequently in competitive athletes than in recreational athletes (13.5% vs. 1.0%; p = 0.001). Clavicle fractures occurred predominantly during competition and non-specific knee injuries during training. Mean time loss ranged from 6.5 weeks for hand fractures to 13.3 weeks for shoulder dislocations. Full return to pre-injury performance ranged from 85.7% after hand fractures to 28.6% after acromioclavicular (AC) joint separations.
CONCLUSION: Injury patterns differed by discipline and setting, suggesting that prevention strategies should address both. The low rate of full return to performance after AC joint separations despite moderate time loss underlines the importance of distinguishing return to sport from return to performance in rehabilitation.

title: Cold-Water Immersion for Post-exercise Recovery: An Overlap-Aware Umbrella Review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cold-water immersion (CWI) is widely used after strenuous exercise, but review-level findings vary by outcome, comparator, recovery window, population, and protocol. Reuse of the same primary studies across reviews can also exaggerate apparent consistency.
METHODS: We searched PubMed, Web of Science, SPORTDiscus, Cochrane Library, Embase, and Scopus from inception to 30 January 2026 for systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and network meta-analyses of post-exercise CWI. Fourteen reviews were included. Primary-study overlap was quantified using the corrected covered area (CCA) overall and for outcome-specific study-to-review mappings. Because overlap was high and review-level estimates were statistically dependent, we did not perform second-order meta-analysis. Source-verified estimates were synthesized in a structured, overlap-aware format. Methodological quality was assessed with AMSTAR 2.
RESULTS: Of the 14 included reviews, 13 provided quantitative estimates, whereas one review provided narrative evidence on heart rate variability (HRV). Overall CCA was 12.68% (high); 99 of 165 primary-study families appeared in at least two reviews. Outcome-specific CCA was 15.03% for delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS; very high) and ranged from 0.00% for interleukin-6 (IL-6) to 25.00% for C-reactive protein (CRP). It was not calculable for HRV, because one review contributed. AMSTAR 2 confidence was low in 2 reviews and critically low in 12. DOMS showed the most consistent favorable pattern: source-review standardized mean differences ranged from -1.04 to -0.37, although the largest estimate was soccer-specific and its 95% prediction interval crossed zero. Because DOMS evidence was highly redundant across the contributing reviews, this apparent consistency does not represent independent replications. Findings for objective performance and biochemical outcomes were inconsistent, time-dependent, or comparator-dependent.
CONCLUSIONS: Within the available review-level evidence, CWI was associated with the most consistent reduction in self-reported short-term post-exercise DOMS, but the clinical importance of the observed effects remains uncertain. Evidence does not support a uniform benefit across objective performance or inflammatory outcomes. Protocol observations, including commonly studied temperatures and durations, are descriptive and should not be interpreted as an optimized prescription. Trial Registration PROSPERO CRD420261332482.

title: Short-term Rhodiola rosea supplementation improves premenstrual symptoms, reaction time, and perceived exertion in female taekwondo athletes: a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Premenstrual symptoms may negatively influence psychological readiness, cognitive-motor performance, and perceived exertion in female athletes. Rhodiola rosea (RR) is an adaptogenic herb that has been investigated for its potential effects on fatigue, stress tolerance, mood, and exercise-related outcomes. However, its effects on premenstrual symptoms and performance-related responses in female athletes remain unclear. This study aimed to investigate the effects of short-term RR supplementation during the estimated symptomatic premenstrual phase on premenstrual symptoms, peripheral serum serotonin and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) concentrations, reaction time, perceived exertion, and aerobic performance-related indices in female taekwondo athletes with premenstrual syndrome (PMS).
METHODS: In this randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 24 female taekwondo athletes with moderate-to-severe PMS symptoms were randomly assigned to receive either 500 mg/day of standardised RR extract (n = 12) or placebo (n = 12) for 10 days during the estimated symptomatic premenstrual phase. Premenstrual symptoms were assessed using the Premenstrual Symptoms Screening Tool (PSST). Visual reaction time, peripheral serum serotonin and GABA concentrations, time to exhaustion (TTE), estimated VO₂max, and rating of perceived exertion (RPE) were evaluated before and after the intervention. Data were analysed using analysis of covariance with baseline values as covariates.
RESULTS: Compared with placebo, RR supplementation significantly reduced several PMS symptoms, including irritability, depression, anxiety, social withdrawal, decreased concentration, hypersomnia, food cravings, crying, skin problems, and abdominal pain (p < 0.05). The RR group demonstrated faster reaction time compared with placebo (adjusted mean difference: -60 ms; p < 0.001). Peripheral serum serotonin and GABA concentrations were significantly higher in the RR group than in the placebo group (p < 0.001). In addition, RR supplementation reduced post-exercise RPE (adjusted mean difference: -1.40 Borg units; p = 0.006). However, no significant differences were observed between groups in TTE or estimated VO₂max (p > 0.05).
CONCLUSION: Short-term RR supplementation during the estimated symptomatic premenstrual phase may improve selected PMS symptoms, visual reaction time, and perceived exertion in female taekwondo athletes with PMS. Larger trials with hormonal confirmation of menstrual cycle phase, longer intervention periods, direct physiological measurements, and sport-specific performance assessments are required to confirm these findings.

title: Effects of different recovery and regeneration modalities on delayed-onset muscle soreness and post-exercise muscle damage markers: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study employed a systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis to compare the effects of multiple post-exercise interventions during the early recovery period, examine whether these effects varied across recovery time points, and provide evidence to inform the selection of post-exercise recovery strategies.
METHODS: PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science were systematically searched, and randomized controlled trials, including parallel-group and crossover designs, were included. A Bayesian random-effects network meta-analysis was used to estimate mean differences (MDs) and 95% credible intervals (CrIs). The revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomized trials (RoB 2) and the Confidence in Network Meta-Analysis (CINeMA) framework were used to assess risk of bias and confidence in the evidence, respectively. Sensitivity analyses and exploratory univariable network meta-regression analyses were also performed.
RESULTS: A total of 35 studies were included in this review. For delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS), whole-body cryotherapy (WBC) and photobiomodulation/phototherapy-related interventions (PHO) showed relatively large reductions in soreness at both 24 and 48 h after exercise. Compared with the combined control/placebo condition (CON/PBO), the effect estimates for WBC were MD = -38.92 (95% CrI: -69.08 to -9.15) at 24 h and MD = -40.03 (95% CrI: -67.74 to -12.44) at 48 h. The corresponding estimates for PHO were MD = -18.20 (95% CrI: -32.91 to -3.72) and MD = -19.46 (95% CrI: -33.55 to -5.99), respectively. For creatine kinase (CK), low-level laser therapy (LLLT) and PHO were associated with lower CK levels at both 24 and 48 h, with the largest estimated effect for LLLT at 48 h (MD = -499.96, 95% CrI: -831.59 to -203.59). For interleukin-6 (IL-6), CWI showed favorable estimates at both 24 and 48 h, although the evidence base was limited and the network was sparse.
CONCLUSION: WBC and PHO showed relatively consistent favorable effects on DOMS at 24 and 48 h, whereas LLLT and PHO showed relatively consistent associations with lower CK levels. The IL-6 findings should be interpreted as exploratory because of the limited evidence base. Selection of post-exercise recovery strategies should consider the target outcome, recovery time window, evidence certainty, and network structure.

title: Sex-Equitable Machine Learning Prediction of Ankle Reinjury in Individuals with Chronic Ankle Instability: A 2-Year Prospective Cohort Study with Fairness Audit.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patients with chronic ankle instability (CAI) face a 2-year reinjury rate approaching 50%, but individualized prediction models that quantify which baseline impairments predict subsequent reinjury within an established CAI cohort remain scarce, and existing prediction models for ankle injury have not assessed sex-related fairness. The aim was to develop and internally validate sex-equitable machine learning (ML) models predicting 2-year ankle reinjury in individuals with CAI, identify the most influential baseline prognostic markers, and audit sex-stratified model performance.
METHODS: One hundred physically active individuals (50 male, 50 female) with CAI (mean age 21.8 ± 2.3 years) were recruited from a university population between February 2017 and February 2018 and prospectively followed for 2 years; 96 (49 male, 47 female) with at least one follow-up response were retained for analysis (41 reinjury events, 43% reinjury rate). Fourteen baseline predictors spanning demographic, anthropometric, injury-history, patient-reported, biomechanical, postural-control, and functional-performance domains were collected. Six algorithms were trained with nested cross-validation: an unpenalized logistic regression baseline and five ML algorithms (Elastic Net, support vector machine, random forest, XGBoost, LightGBM). Predictive contribution of each feature was quantified using Shapley additive explanations and partial-dependence plots. A pre-specified fairness audit compared single global and sex-specific Youden thresholds derived out-of-fold using the equalized-odds gap and disproportionate-impact ratio.
RESULTS: All algorithms achieved area under the curve (AUC) values above 0.70; Elastic Net was selected as the primary model (AUC = 0.807, 95% CI 0.714-0.893; calibration slope = 1.015). Sex, arch height index, previous sprains, dorsiflexion range of motion, and Biodex Overall Stability Index consistently emerged as the most influential prognostic markers. Within-sex discrimination was comparable between males and females, but a single global threshold produced an equalized-odds gap of 0.384 that was reduced by 57% (to 0.164) through sex-specific thresholding without retraining the model.
CONCLUSIONS: ML models with a fairness-audited threshold strategy predicted 2-year ankle reinjury in individuals with CAI, reducing the equalized-odds gap by 57%, though the disproportionate-impact ratio (0.683) remained below the 0.80 benchmark. External validation is required before clinical deployment.

title: Associations between demographic characteristics and Big Five personality traits after anterior cruciate ligament injury: A registry-based cross-sectional study.
abstract:
PURPOSE: The purpose of this study was to investigate associations between demographic characteristics and personality traits, measured with the Big Five Inventory-2 (BFI-2), in patients after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury. A secondary exploratory purpose was to compare demographic characteristics across groups defined by predominant personality trait.
METHODS: Data for this cross-sectional study were obtained from a Swedish rehabilitation-specific registry. Patients aged 15-65 years who completed the Swedish version of the BFI-2 were included. The five BFI-2 domains (extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, open-mindedness and negative emotionality) were analysed as continuous outcomes using multivariable linear regression with sex, age at injury or ACL reconstruction, body mass index (BMI), number of ACL injuries and preinjury Tegner activity level as predictors. Predominant personality trait groups were compared in a secondary exploratory analysis.
RESULTS: A total of 782 patients were included, of whom 692 had complete data for the regression analyses. Female sex was associated with higher scores in all five BFI-2 domains (all p ≤ 0.045). Older age was associated with higher extraversion, conscientiousness and open-mindedness and lower negative emotionality (all p ≤ 0.006). Higher BMI was associated with lower conscientiousness (p = 0.004) and higher open-mindedness (p = 0.049). The models explained 2.7%-13.0% of the variance in personality scores. In the secondary analysis, Agreeableness was the most common predominant trait, and patients classified as predominantly open-minded were older than patients in the other groups.
CONCLUSIONS: Sex and age were associated with several BFI-2 personality traits after ACL injury, whereas BMI showed only small associations. However, demographic characteristics explained little of the variance in personality scores, indicating that personality cannot be reliably inferred from demographic characteristics alone.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

title: The longitudinal relationship between physical capacity and self-perceived physical functioning after total hip and knee arthroplasty.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To examine longitudinal within-person effects between capacity and self-perceived performance during postoperative physiotherapy in patients with total hip and knee arthroplasty (THA/TKA).
METHODS: We performed a secondary analysis of a cluster randomized controlled trial on physiotherapy after THA and TKA using random intercept cross lagged panel models. Capacity was assessed with the 40-m fast-paced walk test (40 m FPWT) and the 30-s chair-stand test (30-s CST), and self-perceived performance with the Oxford Hip/Knee Score functioning subscale (OHS/OKS) and the Hip disability/Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score-Physical function Short form (HOOS-PS/KOOS-PS). Assessments were performed preoperatively and at 3 and 12 months postoperatively.
RESULTS: 312 THA (mean age 66, SD: 9; 53% female) and 312 TKA (mean age 67, SD: 8; 55% female) were included. From pre-surgery to 3 months, no effects were found between capacity and self-perceived performance in either THA or TKA.From 3 to 12 months, in THA, 40 m FPWT performance at 3 months had a positive effect (β 0.34, 95% CI 0.05-0.63) on HOOS-PS scores at 12 months. In TKA, 40 m FPWT performance at 3 months had a positive effect on both OKS functioning (β 0.24 95% CI 0.05-0.43) and KOOS-PS (β 0.29 95% CI 0.11-0.47) scores at 12 months. No other effects were observed.
CONCLUSION: From pre-surgery to 3 months, capacity and self-perceived performance showed no effects within individuals. However, during the early postoperative phase, gait speed may be a relevant treatment target to improve long-term self-perceived performance.

title: Effects of Oral L-Arginine on Everyday Persistent Fatigue, Sleep, and Post-Exercise Lactate Recovery in Community-Dwelling Working-Age Adults: A Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Randomized Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: The evidence for nutritional interventions against fatigue is limited; we evaluated whether L-arginine reduces fatigue in working-age adults.
METHODS: In this 8-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 120 community-dwelling working-age adults aged 30-59 years with persistent fatigue (Fatigue Severity Scale [FSS] total ≥ 27) received oral L-arginine 3 g/day, 6 g/day, or placebo. The primary endpoint was FSS change; secondary endpoints included the Checklist Individual Strength (CIS), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and blood lactate kinetics during a standardized submaximal treadmill run (~70% VO2max, 30 min). Data from 119 participants were analyzed, with Holm adjustment for multiplicity.
RESULTS: At Week 8, FSS decreased more with 6 g/day than with placebo (-6.41 vs. -2.23; Holm-adjusted p = 0.024), whereas 3 g/day did not differ from placebo. The 6 g/day CIS improvement did not survive multiplicity adjustment. PSQI scores improved nominally at both doses (3 g/day, p = 0.007; 6 g/day, p = 0.045). With 6 g/day, the total lactate area under the curve (Holm-adjusted p = 0.041) and 15-min recovery lactate (Holm-adjusted p = 0.002) were lower than with the placebo, whereas the resting plasma nitrite did not differ. No serious adverse events occurred.
CONCLUSIONS: L-arginine supplementation at 6 g/day for 8 weeks reduced fatigue severity relative to placebo and was well-tolerated; however, mean FSS scores remained above the enrollment threshold, indicating a reduction in, rather than resolution of, persistent fatigue.

title: Orthobiologics for hand and wrist disorders: An indication-specific systematic review and evidence-gap synthesis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Orthobiologics are increasingly used in hand and wrist disorders; however, their clinical effectiveness remains uncertain due to heterogeneity in indications, formulations, and outcome reporting.
METHODS: This systematic review was reported in accordance with PRISMA 2020 and prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261359867). PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, and Web of Science were searched from inception through March 31, 2026. Primary clinical studies evaluating locally delivered orthobiologics for hand or wrist disorders were eligible. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2 for randomized trials and ROBINS-I for nonrandomized comparative studies and the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist for uncontrolled case series; certainty was evaluated using GRADE. Because the studies differed substantially in indication, biologic formulation, comparator, follow-up, and outcome definition, meta-analysis was not clinically appropriate; a structured qualitative synthesis was performed.
RESULTS: Ten primary clinical studies were included: three studies of carpal tunnel syndrome, one of de Quervain tenosynovitis, three of trapeziometacarpal osteoarthritis, one of distal-radius fracture, and two of scaphoid nonunion. No meta-analysis was performed. Evidence for carpal tunnel syndrome was inconsistent across comparators and follow-up durations. In de Quervain tenosynovitis, PRP produced outcomes comparable to corticosteroid injection, with fewer reported local adverse effects. Evidence for trapeziometacarpal osteoarthritis was limited and comparator-dependent. In scaphoid nonunion, the primary BMP studies suggested possible osteoinductive benefit but also identified complications, including heterotopic ossification, persistent nonunion, and reoperation. Overall certainty ranged from moderate to very low.
CONCLUSIONS: Orthobiologic effectiveness for hand and wrist disorders appears indication-specific but is supported by limited and heterogeneous evidence. Routine PRP use in osteoarthritis is not supported, and application in other conditions should remain selective and context-dependent. Larger, adequately powered, placebo-controlled trials with standardized biologic characterization and outcome reporting are required. These findings should be interpreted as an evidence-gap map rather than proof of comparative efficacy.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV (systematic review of predominantly small randomized and nonrandomized studies with heterogeneous designs and limited sample sizes).

title: Eight-week omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation alters but does not attenuate exercise-induced muscle damage in older adults: a randomised controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) serves as a model to study muscle plasticity and recovery. Exercise recovery declines with age, and while omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (n-3 PUFA) exhibit inconsistent effects in younger adults, the effect in older adults is unknown.
METHODS: In a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial, 43 healthy, older women and men (65-85 years) ingested 5 mL of n-3 PUFA algae oil (2 g PUFA) or placebo for eight weeks. After eight weeks participants performed a bout of 10 × 10 eccentric-emphasised leg extensions. Outcome measures included quadriceps maximal voluntary contraction (MVC), muscle soreness, creatine kinase (CK) and inflammation (Interleukin-6, high-sensitive C-reactive protein; CRP) assessed at baseline and post-exercise.
RESULTS: EIMD symptoms such as muscle soreness and function were modest and consistent with previous reports in older adults. Overall, n-3 PUFA supplementation did not improve functional recovery. However, a borderline greater MVC loss was observed in the n-3 PUFA group (time × group: P = .064), which resulted from significantly lower MVC in the n-3 PUFA group at 24 h (difference: -10.9%, 95%CI: -21.4;-0.40%, P = .042) and at 72 h (difference: -9.80, 95%CI: -18.3;-1.27, P = .025) post-exercise compared to the placebo. No significant overall group differences were observed for CK, interleukin-6, CRP, but CK concentrations significantly increased from baseline at 24 h post-exercise in the placebo group (change: +81.1%, 95%CI:10.5;152%, P = .014). Habitual physical activity and sex emerged as significant moderators of molecular recovery in an exploratory analysis.
CONCLUSION: n-3 PUFA supplementation did not improve functional recovery, but different molecular response patterns were observed. Habitual physical activity and sex may be determinants of post-exercise response; this exploratory finding warrants confirmation in larger studies.

title: Age-Related Patterns of Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) Symptoms and Key Performance Factors in Adolescent Biathletes.
abstract: Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) impairs health and performance, but age-related patterns in its emergence remain unclear. This study examines RED symptoms in adolescent biathletes at season-start and their link to end-of-season performance. A national cross-sectional study including prospective performance registration recruited biathletes to complete validated questionnaires, followed by clinical interviews if eating disorders (EDs) were indicated. Athletes ≥ 18 years were invited for physical laboratory assessments. End-of-season results were retrieved from open records. Analyses were performed by elastic net regression to identify the most stable predictors of performance, which were finally included in a linear regression model. Seventy-two athletes (55% females) with mean (SD) age 17.8 (1.4) years, 13.3 (3.3) training hours/week, and representing median (min, max) tier 3.0 (2, 5) were included. Prevalence in symptoms of low energy availability (LEA) was 18%, REDs 32%, EDs 11% (20% among females), and of depression 15%. Among 28 athletes (43% female) completing laboratory assessments, 11% had low BMD and ≤ 25% had clinical metabolic markers. Symptoms of mental health issues and REDs were more common in females and the older age groups. Higher training volume and low RED severity positively predicted performance, whereas injury/illness-related training absences, cholesterol, and body fat percentage negatively affected race results. RED symptoms are common in young biathletes. Illness/injury-related training absences were frequent and linked to poorer end-of-season performance, underscoring the need for routine screening by health- and performance teams to detect and manage early symptoms of LEA, reduce RED risk, and prevent premature career termination.

title: Effects of Whey Protein Supplementation on Muscle Damage, Hepatic Stress, and Inflammatory Markers in Power- and Endurance-Trained Athletes.
abstract: This study investigated the effects of 8 weeks of whey protein supplementation (30 g/day) on biomarkers of liver function, inflammation, and muscle damage in trained power-trained (predominantly speed-power/anaerobic-power disciplines) and endurance-trained athletes, in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled design. Fifty-nine male athletes were stratified into power (n = 30) and endurance (n = 29) groups, then randomly assigned to a whey protein group (WG) or a placebo control group (CG). Biomarkers assessed pre- and post-intervention included alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), C-reactive protein (CRP), and creatine kinase (CK). Significant reductions in ALT, AST, and CK were observed in both endurance- and power-trained athletes after supplementation (p = 0.001, p = 0.015, p = 0.001, and p = 0.003 respectively), indicating attenuated hepatic and muscular stress. Among the four biomarkers, only ALT displayed a statistically significant three-way interaction (Time × Supplementation × Training modality; p = 0.003), identifying it as the sole marker showing a genuine modality-specific differential response to supplementation. A significant within-group reduction in CRP was additionally observed in the supplemented power-trained athletes (p = 0.039), whereas endurance athletes showed only minor, non-significant changes; because the omnibus three-way interaction for CRP was not significant, this finding is reported as a within-group trend rather than evidence of a differential effect between modalities. Placebo groups demonstrated stable or increased enzyme and CRP values, particularly in endurance athletes. These findings suggest that whey protein may attenuate exercise-induced hepatic and muscular stress across training modalities, with a modality-specific effect on hepatic stress markers (ALT) observed in power-trained athletes. The results highlight whey protein's potential as a nutritional aid to promote recovery and physiological adaptation, possibly mediated by antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanisms. Further studies are warranted to examine long-term outcomes and dose-response effects across different training profiles.

title: Platelet Concentrates in Tooth Replantation: A Narrative Review and Evidence Synthesis of Periodontal and Pulpal Healing.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: The prognosis of an avulsed, replanted tooth over the long term hinges on whether the periodontal ligament (PDL) and the dental pulp can be preserved or regenerated. When extra-oral dry time is prolonged, PDL necrosis follows, and the root becomes prone to inflammatory or replacement (ankylotic) resorption. Platelet concentrates-platelet-rich plasma (PRP), leukocyte- and platelet-rich plasma (L-PRP), and platelet-rich fibrin (PRF)-are autologous biomaterials that supply growth factors and may influence this healing process. This review asks whether autologous platelet concentrates reduce inflammatory and replacement (ankylotic) root resorption and improve periodontal and pulpal healing after delayed or intentional tooth replantation, compared with no adjunct, and whether residual periodontal ligament (PDL) viability changes this effect.
MATERIAL AND METHODS: This narrative synthesis (not a systematic review) draws together recent controlled clinical and animal studies with the case-report and preclinical literature already captured in the only published systematic review on this topic. The search covered PubMed, Google Scholar, the Cochrane Library, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science, from January to May 2026.
RESULTS: In preclinical models, L-PRP and PRF promote pulpal repair, tertiary dentin formation, and attenuated inflammatory root resorption, although neither consistently prevents ankylosis once PDL viability has been lost. In one retrospective comparative study of intentional replantation in hopeless teeth, PRF combined with root-surface biomodification produced greater clinical attachment gain and a larger reduction in probing depth than replantation alone, a direction consistent with earlier case reports. Small, largely non-randomized samples and unstandardized protocols still limit this evidence.
CONCLUSIONS: Platelet concentrates are biologically plausible adjuncts that improve periodontal and pulpal healing indices, yet they do not reliably prevent ankylosis. Their clinical role will remain undefined until prospective randomized trials with standardized protocols are available.
